nameStory: This little aquatic plant gets its "water-starwort" name from its star-shaped leaf clusters that float on water surfaces like tiny green constellations. The "narrow-fruited" part refers to its slender seed pods, which help distinguish it from its plumper-fruited cousins in quiet ponds and streams.
description: Narrow-fruited Water-starwort is a delicate aquatic plant that lives both underwater and floating on the surface. It forms small rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves that create star-like patterns on calm water, while its submerged portions have thin, linear leaves. This tiny plant rarely grows more than a few inches across, making it easy to overlook among larger pond weeds and water lilies.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two distinct leaf types: floating leaves are small, oval, and spoon-shaped in star-like rosettes, while underwater leaves are thin and linear like grass blades

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small mats or patches on water surface, with delicate stems that feel soft and squishy when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous flowers without petals that appear in leaf axils - so small you'll need to look very closely to spot them

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, narrow seed pods that are distinctly slender compared to related species - about the size of a pinhead

habitat: Look for this plant in shallow, quiet waters like pond edges, slow streams, ditches, and seasonal pools throughout New England. It prefers areas with soft, muddy bottoms and can tolerate both temporary flooding and occasional drying. You'll often find it mixed with other small aquatic plants in areas that cattle or wildlife visit to drink.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as water warms, with fresh green rosettes appearing on the surface. This is when the plant is most visible and easiest to identify.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom inconspicuously while the plant reaches peak size. Star-shaped leaf clusters are most prominent during warm months.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline as temperatures cool, with some leaves turning brownish. Seeds develop and disperse during this time.
seasonality.winter: Most above-water growth dies back, though some plants may persist in protected areas or warmer microclimates. Seeds overwinter in mud.

funFact: This tiny water plant is a master of adaptation - it can completely change its leaf shape depending on whether it's growing underwater or on the surface, essentially becoming two different-looking plants in one!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other water-starworts, especially Pond Water-starwort, but the narrow, slender fruits are the key distinguishing feature. Remember: "narrow name, narrow fruits" - if the seed pods look plump and round, you're looking at a different species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "water-starwort," this plant isn't related to the terrestrial starworts (Stellaria species) that grow in gardens and woodlands. The name similarity is purely coincidental, based on the star-like appearance of both plant groups.
compareHints: Among New England's water-starworts, Narrow-fruited Water-starwort has the slenderest seed pods, while Pond Water-starwort has rounder, broader fruits. Large Water-starwort is noticeably bigger overall with larger floating leaves, and Terrestrial Water-starwort can actually grow on muddy shores rather than requiring standing water.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pond water-starwort differs from its relatives like narrow-fruited water-starwort by preferring completely still water rather than flowing streams.

Large Water-starwort differs from its relatives like Narrow-fruited Water-starwort mainly in the size and arrangement of its floating leaves - it has broader leaves in more prominent star-shaped clusters.

Unlike its aquatic relatives like Pond Water-starwort and Large Water-starwort, Terrestrial Water-starwort has adapted to completely dry conditions and forms ground-hugging mats rather than floating rosettes.
